hints: Look at the polymer backbone and remember that one addition monomer always gives a two-carbon section in the chain.
The two-carbon repeat is $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-}$, so the original monomer must have been $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$.
Work out the $M_r$ of that small alkene, then divide 10000 by it to find how many monomers fit in one chain.
walkthrough:
**Spot the repeat unit in the diagram**

The diagram shows a chain of $\text{-CH}_2\text{-}$ groups. In addition polymerisation, each C=C double bond opens to make two single bonds.

So one monomer gives two backbone carbons:
$$\text{monomer } \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \rightarrow \text{ polymer section -CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-}$$

**Find the $M_r$ of the monomer**

The monomer is ethene, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$. Add up the atoms with $C=12$ and $H=1$.

$$M_r = (2 \times 12) + (4 \times 1) = 24 + 4 = 28$$

**Divide to find number of monomers**

The whole polymer $M_r$ is about 10000. Divide by the mass of one monomer.

$$\text{number of monomers} = \frac{10000}{28} \approx 357$$

This is approximately 360 joined monomers in each molecule.

options.A: 180 comes from using the four-carbon length shown as one monomer. That four-carbon piece has mass about 56, and 10000 / 56 is about 180. But the diagram shows two monomer units joined, not one, so the monomer mass is only 28.
options.B: 360 is correct. The monomer is ethene, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$, with $M_r = 28$. Dividing the polymer mass by the monomer mass, 10000 / 28 is about 357, which is approximately 360.
options.C: 625 comes from dividing 10000 by 16. That is the $M_r$ of methane, $\text{CH}_4$, not ethene. It is a mistake in calculating the monomer mass, probably by miscounting C and H atoms.
options.D: 710 comes from dividing 10000 by 14. That is the mass of one $\text{-CH}_2\text{-}$ repeat group, not a whole monomer. An addition monomer must supply two carbons, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$, so you must divide by 28, not 14.
